A new documentary on Apple TV, "All of Us," tells the story of a public elementary school that takes a unique approach to educating students with vastly different needs.

The iPhone and iPad are key tools that make this model, hailed as a powerful example of inclusive education, possible—ensuring every child can benefit……

Students with special needs require additional support due to disabilities, and traditionally they have been taught separately from mainstream students. Conventional thinking holds that bringing everyone into the same classroom would be disruptive to the majority of students.

Ruby Bridges Elementary took the opposite approach, and the results proved that inclusive learning not only avoids disruption but actually benefits all students academically and socially. The model was so successful that the school's principal and a kindergarten teacher were both selected as Principal of the Year and Teacher of the Year in 2025.

A 70-minute documentary is now streaming on Apple TV, telling the story of "a school that breaks the mould."

At Ruby Bridges, all students learn together in general education classrooms. Every child does math together, reads together, and sings together in music class. Teachers and specialists work side by side in the classroom, and the results speak for themselves. So how do they do it? Ruby Bridges Elementary is a public school, with no extra funding or additional staff beyond what a typical school would have. There's no magic formula—just a group of educators who decided to stop separating children and chose to believe in the power of learning together. This is the story of a school that breaks the mould: a school that is unique, but shouldn't have to be.

The iPad and iPhone play a key role

Some students have severe communication difficulties, and augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) software running on the iPad and iPhone has dramatically improved their ability to communicate with teachers and classmates.

A major discovery was that AAC apps don't just help students with communication challenges—they're useful for all students. The founding principal told me at the time:

All students—whether they have strong literacy and language skills, or they're just beginning to learn to communicate or use language—show high levels of engagement when they can use AAC tools to generate, expand on, or express their ideas. When we have a tool that supports communication while also overcoming barriers in the classroom and in life, we can bypass challenges with motor skills, writing stamina, and even the anxiety of speaking out loud……This really is the best embodiment of what we call 'universal design'—more so than almost any other language, communication, or vocabulary tool we've used in the classroom, this is a tool that belongs to everyone.

As the documentary reveals, this model works not only for students with special needs but for all students, and that's beyond dispute. A website set up for the documentary also offers a rich collection of video resources for other schools interested in following Ruby Bridges' example.
